timeline.title: Born on Milk Street
timeline.text: Benjamin Franklin was born on Milk Street in Boston, the son of a candle and soap maker. By the calendar then used in England it was 6 January 1705; by today's calendar it was 17 January 1706. He was, he wrote, the youngest son of the youngest son for five generations.

timeline.title: School ends at ten
timeline.text: He attended Boston Latin School but did not graduate. His formal schooling ended when he was 10. After that he taught himself, mostly from books.

timeline.title: Apprentice printer
timeline.text: At 12 he was apprenticed to his older brother James, a printer. He taught himself to write by rewriting essays from The Spectator magazine and comparing his versions with the originals.

timeline.title: Silence Dogood
timeline.text: He slipped letters under the door of his brother's newspaper, the New-England Courant, signed 'Silence Dogood', a made-up middle-aged widow. When James was jailed that year, Ben ran the paper.

timeline.title: Runs away to Philadelphia
timeline.text: He broke his apprenticeship and ran away. He arrived in Philadelphia almost penniless and, by his own account, walked up Market Street with a roll of bread under each arm, eating a third.

timeline.title: Stranded in London
timeline.text: Promised letters of credit that never came, he found himself in London and worked as a typesetter in print shops there. He came back to Philadelphia in 1726.

timeline.title: The Junto
timeline.text: He formed the Junto, a club of young tradesmen who met on Friday evenings to debate questions and read essays, in a spirit of inquiry rather than argument.

timeline.title: The Pennsylvania Gazette
timeline.text: After opening a print shop with Hugh Meredith in 1728, he became publisher of the Pennsylvania Gazette. Like other printers of the time, he also earned money from paid advertisements, including ads for the sale of enslaved people.

timeline.title: Marriage and a son
timeline.text: He entered a common-law marriage with Deborah Read. He publicly acknowledged a son, William, born the same year.

timeline.title: The Library Company
timeline.text: Franklin and fellow Junto members signed the articles that founded the Library Company of Philadelphia, a lending library that pooled members' money to buy books. It still exists.

timeline.title: Poor Richard's Almanack
timeline.text: Writing as 'Richard Saunders', he published the first Poor Richard's Almanack. He kept it going until 1758, selling up to 10,000 copies a year. Most of its proverbs came from older books, reworded.

timeline.title: An enslaver
timeline.text: From at least 1735 and for decades after, Franklin owned enslaved people, at least seven over his life, including two men who worked in his household and shop. His newspaper ran ads for sales of enslaved people. This is part of his record and is stated here plainly.

timeline.title: Loss of Francis, and a fire company
timeline.text: His young son Francis, born in 1732, died of smallpox. The same year Franklin created the Union Fire Company, one of the first volunteer fire companies in America, and became clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly.

timeline.title: The Franklin stove
timeline.text: He designed an iron fireplace to heat rooms with less wood and described it in a 1744 pamphlet. Offered a patent, he refused it. The design drew poorly, and David Rittenhouse later improved it.

timeline.title: American Philosophical Society
timeline.text: He helped found the American Philosophical Society to share useful knowledge. He became its first president in 1769.

timeline.title: Stepping back from printing
timeline.text: He went into partnership with his foreman David Hall, who ran the shop and paid Franklin half the profits for 18 years. That gave Franklin time for science and public life.

timeline.title: An academy for Philadelphia
timeline.text: He became first president of the Academy of Philadelphia, which opened in 1751 and later grew into the University of Pennsylvania.

timeline.title: The kite and the lightning rod
timeline.text: In June, by Joseph Priestley's later account, Franklin flew a kite near a storm to show that lightning is electricity. The kite was charged from the clouds, not struck. Lightning rods were put up on the Academy and the State House that year.

timeline.title: The Copley Medal
timeline.text: The Royal Society in London gave him its Copley Medal for his work on electricity. That year he also became deputy postmaster general for the British colonies in North America.

timeline.title: The Albany Plan
timeline.text: At the Albany Congress he proposed a plan to unite the colonies under one council. It was not adopted.

timeline.title: Agent in London
timeline.text: The Pennsylvania Assembly sent him to London as its agent. He lived in England for most of the next 18 years. He took two enslaved men, Peter and King, with him. By the late 1750s he had begun to argue against slavery.

timeline.title: The Way to Wealth
timeline.text: His last almanac opened with 'Father Abraham's Speech', a string of Poor Richard's sayings on work and thrift. Reprinted as The Way to Wealth, it became popular on both sides of the Atlantic.

timeline.title: The glass armonica
timeline.text: After hearing music played on water-filled glasses, he built the armonica, a row of spinning glass bowls played with wet fingers. Mozart and Beethoven later wrote music for it.

timeline.title: Against the Stamp Act
timeline.text: He testified before Parliament against the Stamp Act tax on the colonies, which was repealed that year.

timeline.title: Humiliated before the Privy Council
timeline.text: After Franklin passed on private letters of Massachusetts governor Thomas Hutchinson, which were leaked in 1773, the Solicitor-General Alexander Wedderburn ridiculed him before the Privy Council. His post as deputy postmaster general ended days later.

timeline.title: Deborah dies
timeline.text: His wife Deborah died in Philadelphia while he was still in Britain.

timeline.title: Home to a revolution
timeline.text: Back in America, he joined the Second Continental Congress and became the first Postmaster General of the United Colonies.

timeline.title: The Declaration
timeline.text: He helped draft and signed the Declaration of Independence, then sailed to France to seek its help in the war.

timeline.title: Alliance with France
timeline.text: Popular in Paris, he secured a military alliance with France that proved critical to winning the war.

timeline.title: The Treaty of Paris
timeline.text: He helped negotiate and signed the treaty in which Britain recognised American independence.

timeline.title: Home, and freeing his slaves
timeline.text: Back from France, he was chosen President of Pennsylvania. After his return he became an abolitionist and freed the two enslaved people he still held.

timeline.title: Abolition society and the Constitution
timeline.text: He became president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society. That summer he was a delegate to the Constitutional Convention, though he chose not to raise slavery publicly there.

timeline.title: Petition to end slavery
timeline.text: As the society's president he signed a petition asking the first Congress to abolish slavery and the slave trade. Pro-slavery members attacked it, and the House tabled it.

timeline.title: Death in Philadelphia
timeline.text: Franklin died at 84 and was buried at Christ Church Burial Ground. His will asked for a grave marked 'Benjamin and Deborah Franklin'.

timeline.title: The lost Gulf Stream chart
timeline.text: A researcher found an original of Franklin's 1770 chart of the Gulf Stream, made to help ships cross the Atlantic faster, in the national library in Paris.

works.title: The Silence Dogood letters
works.text: Witty letters in the voice of a made-up widow, printed in his brother's newspaper when he was 16.

works.title: The Junto
works.text: A weekly club for mutual improvement that debated questions and later launched a library.

works.title: The Pennsylvania Gazette
works.text: The newspaper he published in Philadelphia for many years.

works.title: Library Company of Philadelphia
works.text: A members' lending library, an offshoot of the Junto. It still holds over 2,000 items once owned by Franklin.

works.title: Poor Richard's Almanack
works.text: A yearly almanac of weather, dates and proverbs, published under the name Richard Saunders until 1758.

works.title: Union Fire Company
works.text: One of the first volunteer fire companies in America.

works.title: The Franklin stove
works.text: An iron fireplace meant to warm a room with less fuel. He refused a patent so anyone could make it.

works.title: American Philosophical Society
works.text: A society for sharing useful knowledge, still active in Philadelphia.

works.title: Academy of Philadelphia
works.text: The school he led, which grew into the University of Pennsylvania.

works.title: The lightning rod
works.text: A pointed metal rod that leads lightning safely to the ground. Never patented.

works.title: The Albany Plan of Union
works.text: An early proposal to unite the colonies under one council.

works.title: The Way to Wealth
works.text: His best-known collection of Poor Richard's sayings, framed as an old man's speech at an auction.

works.title: The glass armonica
works.text: A musical instrument of spinning glass bowls, played with wet fingers.

works.title: Gulf Stream chart
works.text: One of the first charts of the Gulf Stream, published in London and largely ignored at first.

works.title: Declaration of Independence
works.text: He helped draft and signed it.

works.title: Treaty of Paris
works.text: The peace treaty that ended the war and recognised the United States.

works.title: Bifocals (double spectacles)
works.text: Glasses with split lenses for near and far. He is generally credited, but historians are not sure he was the first; he was at least one of the first to wear them.

works.title: The Autobiography
works.text: His life story up to the late 1750s, begun in 1771, written in parts and left unfinished. It was first published, in French, in 1791.
